Case Vignette: "Mr. A."

Mr. A. is a 35-year-old single man of European descent who has been a special education teacher for the past decade. He presents for therapy at the urging of his school principal, who noticed a sharp decline in his patience and focus over the last four months. Mr. A. agrees he is struggling, but describes his problem as "falling apart at work," not as a trauma reaction.

The event that changed everything occurred five months ago. Mr. A. was walking home from a late parent-teacher conference at 8:30 PM. He was on a well-lit street two blocks from his apartment, carrying a tote bag with student folders and his laptop. He recalls hearing footsteps behind him, then a hand grabbing his collar. A man shoved him against a brick wall, pressed something hard into his ribs (Mr. A. believes it was a knife, though he never saw it), and hissed, "Give me your bag or I'll cut you."

Mr. A. froze. He remembers thinking, I have 27 IEPs in that bag. I cannot lose those files. He did not scream. He did not run. He handed over the bag. The man was gone in seconds. Mr. A. stood against the wall for what felt like minutes, his heart pounding so hard he thought he might vomit. He walked the remaining blocks home, called the police, and filed a report. The bag was never recovered.

For the first two weeks, Mr. A. felt "shaky but fine." He took a single sick day, then returned to work. He did not tell his colleagues what happened—he felt ashamed that he had not fought back or even seen the attacker's face. He replayed the moment of freezing, wondering why he didn't run. "I teach kids to stand up for themselves," he says, his voice flat. "I couldn't even stand up for a laptop."

By the third week, he began to experience intrusive memories. While standing at the whiteboard, he would suddenly feel the cold brick against his back. The smell of damp pavement would trigger a surge of panic. He started avoiding the route home, driving instead, even though his commute tripled. He stopped leaving school after dark, scheduling all meetings before 4 PM. When a student tapped his shoulder unexpectedly, he flinched so violently that the child cried.

His sleep deteriorated. He wakes three to four times a night, often from dreams where he is being chased through the school hallways. He now sleeps with a small dumbbell under his bed—he has never purchased a weapon, but the weight of the metal is comforting. He has stopped jogging in the evenings, his primary stress relief, because he cannot bear the feeling of someone behind him.

At work, his patience has eroded. He has worked for years with non-verbal students with severe autism, a job requiring enormous calm. Now, when a student screams or flaps, Mr. A. feels a flash of irrational rage. He snapped at a 12-year-old last month, shouting, "Just be quiet for one second!" He apologized immediately, but the guilt has not faded. He now feels "on edge" every second of the school day, scanning the classroom for threats that do not exist.

Socially, he has withdrawn. He cancelled a weekend trip with friends, claiming he was sick. He has not dated since the mugging. "I don't want anyone to see me like this," he says. "I used to be the guy who calmed everyone down. Now I can't calm myself down."

His PCL-5 score is 58, indicating severe PTSD symptoms. He has not had a full panic attack, but experiences daily hypervigilance, emotional numbing, and a persistent sense of a foreshortened future—he told me, "I don't plan past next week. What's the point?"

Mr. A. sits in my office with his hands clenched on his knees. He looks exhausted. When I ask what he hopes to get from therapy, he says, "I just want to stop feeling like I'm still on that street."
